tested_scope: One bounded official-GitHub documentation audit of repository incarnation identity for historical tombstone binding: REST id/node_id exposure, global-node-ID uniqueness/reference semantics, rename/transfer continuity signals, delete-or-recreate same-location distinction signals, and quota-zero Chat-accessible read feasibility. No live mutation experiment was performed.

public_sources.observation: The documented repository REST representation includes numeric id and node_id. The Get a repository endpoint for public resources can be used without authentication or with metadata-read permission, subject to normal API rate limits.
GitHub documents node_id as a global node ID obtainable from REST and usable for direct GraphQL node lookup, and recommends persisting global node IDs as object references across API versions.
GitHub documents global IDs as unique opaque references and warns consumers not to decode their format.
Rename preserves repository information and redirects old repository locations; creating a new repository at the former name later destroys that redirect.
Transfer preserves repository contents and associated objects and redirects the previous location; creating a new repository or fork at the previous location permanently removes the redirect.

observations: A repository exposes two machine-readable identity fields, id and node_id, while its owner/name location can change.
Global node IDs are documented as unique opaque object references and are intended to be persisted for later object reference.
Rename and transfer are documented as continuity operations on a repository: associated information remains and old locations redirect to the moved repository.
Reusing a prior repository location by creating a new repository or fork breaks the redirect to the moved repository, which is evidence that location and repository incarnation are separable.

The retrieved official documentation does not explicitly state that a repository's numeric id or node_id is invariant across rename and transfer, nor explicitly state that a delete-and-recreate at the same owner/name can never reuse a prior id/node_id.
inferences: node_id is a stronger candidate incarnation key than owner/name because it is a unique object reference rather than a mutable location.

Combining the uniqueness contract with rename/transfer continuity makes stability across those operations plausible, but that stability was not explicitly guaranteed by the retrieved documentation and therefore is not accepted as proved.

The redirect-destruction rules show that a new repository at an old location is distinguishable operationally from the moved repository, but they do not by themselves prove non-reuse of id/node_id after deletion.
claim_idempotency_implication: A historical tombstone keyed only by owner/name is unsafe under rename/transfer/name reuse. A tombstone keyed by global node_id would avoid location aliasing only if node_id persistence across rename/transfer and non-reuse after delete/recreate are guaranteed or empirically bound by a stronger immutable witness. Current documentation is insufficient for that acceptance claim.

pairing_with_immutable_release_tag_reser.candidate: repository-global-node-id + immutable-release reserved tag or attested release identity
pairing_with_immutable_release_tag_reser.benefit: Would bind the tag tombstone to a repository incarnation rather than mutable owner/name.
pairing_with_immutable_release_tag_reser.reason: Part115 did not prove node_id lifecycle invariants across rename/transfer/delete-recreate, and Part114 already left historical attestation persistence after release deletion unresolved. Pairing two individually incomplete lifecycle proofs cannot establish a complete tombstone binding.

result.falsification: Official documentation was insufficient to prove the full repository-incarnation lifecycle contract needed for a permanent historical tombstone: explicit id/node_id stability across rename/transfer and explicit non-reuse after delete-and-recreate remain undocumented in the retrieved sources.
result.minimal_unresolved_child: Obtain a source-qualified lifecycle proof for repository global node identity, or construct a bounded public read-only redirect experiment that compares the same documented moved repository through old and new locations and then separately identifies a documented delete/recreate case without mutating user repositories.

scope_guard: Only current multi_agent role-local continuation and official public GitHub documentation were used. No O, other worker, downstream, legacy, shared-ledger, scheduler-state, protected-primary or other-role semantic input was read or used.
conflict_check: Single bounded Part115 leaf only; no optional second semantic leaf executed. Repository writes are confined to the authorized multi_agent state/receipt namespaces.
exact_continuation: Part116: execute one bounded public read-only repository-redirect identity experiment, using only official GitHub pages/API responses and no user-repository mutation. Find one source-qualified repository rename or transfer with an old location that still redirects; query old and current locations and compare REST id/node_id to test identity continuity empirically. In the same leaf, treat delete/recreate non-reuse as unresolved unless an official source or existing public case supplies pre/post identities without requiring mutation. If no source-qualified moved repository can be established within the bounded read budget, persist that blocker and make the next distinct candidate an official audit of GraphQL node deletion semantics; do not execute a second leaf in the same invocation.
